title: Criticism of Origene's Interpretation
english: A protection of the law is established from heaven to call for help, not to seek assistance from the earth by looking at earthly things. But Origene, having made it his habit to interpret all the scriptures, does not treat these testimonies as things to be known, nor does he set them down as they ought to be; rather, he circles around those which differ in nothing regarding the matter, yet exceeds those which belong to its own nature; for it seems he does this foolishly through ignorance, or he deals with it boldly through ill-will.

But just as, having spoken in a two-sided way, saying, 'What then does a ventriloquist do here? What does a ventriloquist do concerning the raising up of the soul of the righteous?' (1 Samuel 28:15), he avoided the difficulty of the word by being evasive, he inscribes something else which he himself has done; but having committed the whole matter to the scripture itself, he asserts that Samuel was carried up, yet no longer dares to make secondary the 'who raised him up?' (1 Samuel 28:13).

I think that even later, being investigated by those who always think most correctly, and defending himself a second time, he explained that the place of the ventriloquist had been preserved; then he says also that 'it is written that a ventriloquist raised someone,' and 'that Saul said to Samuel is written.' And, having frequently tautologized such things with much babbling, he brings forth again: 'and it has not been said,' he says, 'whether he went up voluntarily; for you do not have,' he said, 'it lying there if the ventriloquist raised him; let someone who has read the scripture examine it.'

Surely, being investigated as an opponent, he clearly denied what he had previously glorified through thoughtlessness; for there he limited the scripture to having said rather [the thing], but not the woman, the 'whom shall I bring to you?'; and, being clearly caught here, he hurried to escape by hiding the cause.

Thus, having fought for himself and being disgraced, he is stripped naked, as if having been defeated in a contest of knowledge right here and now, seeking a way to escape the blame. Since, being dragged by pain, he admitted that the woman did not lead the prophet's soul, let him say who led it (for he had determined that she alone was to be carried away unchangeably). It happened that the pythian oracle was alone, and Saul, who was serving her, was the master of the prophet. But this one could not be the agent of the drama; for it was not necessary for him to approach the engastrimythos at night like her.

But if the deed has happened, the thing seen must be written for someone else. So it is necessary to say one of two things for the two: either this never happened at all, or the upright man was carried away through the engastrimythos and the demon. Does he then, appearing to deny his own voices by another method, deceptively introduce a presumption of vanity? Rather, through those things by which he seems to defend himself, he introduces falsehood as truth.

He is not convinced by so many and such votes of law, nor by harmonious prophetic testimonies, nor by the remaining consistent concordances of history; but having made a fallacy of the truly holy sayings, he confirms the words of the engastrimythos by his choice, later establishing instruments of idolatry and circling with impious demon-divination. Nor does even the compound name convince him of what kind of conduct it has; for the engastrimythos is interpreted as showing a myth formed in the belly, but the compound of the myth is structured as if dwelling plausibly inside the stomach, shouting not truth but falsehood against it. It is better that those who have spoken with various word-references know at a distance what the kind of it is.
Even if he has introduced Greek divination, which burns most with superstition, as if it were forgotten, nevertheless I think we must not refrain from exposing it from here.

title: The Artificiality of Myth
english: His lack of understanding for a short time, as is necessary.

For rhetorical arts clearly show that a myth is a fabrication composed for entertainment toward some use differing from life; and a fabrication is said to be 'made' from the very fact that it is composed in agreement with itself; for it would no longer be called a myth if it were actually true.

If, however, it is a composition of spontaneous fabrication or myth-making, it may be proven true in deed, but in word it depicts the substance of things with images, lacking in practice; for it seems to plausibly present non-existent things as if they were existing, and its narration introduces a fabricated imitation; therefore, it announces things that are unsubstantial, without any underlying basis being presented as if it were certain.

Moreover, it seems to me that the craft of making a myth does not differ from shadow-painting without soul; for by similarity, I think, the painting is itself characterized by the line; by a near resemblance, it personifies a hypothesis, casting aside one part, while it shapes the others through imitation with prescribed letters. Thus, it observes a lack of agreement in each of its rhythms most strictly, writing both the beginning and end of a war in a plausible manner, and the speaking lips and the peculiarities of voices, and laughter and weeping, or the authoritative speeches of a public forum, or symposia and revelries, or bacchanalia or rites, or unrestrained drinking, or erotic exhortations, or brigand raids, or unseemly destruction, or lawless slaughter, or the acting of poverty, or the flowing of wealth.

Therefore, everything is characterized by economy of expression, and through personification, it approaches and depicts idle actions; for indeed, the myth-makers, selecting words like flowers, produce various kinds of colored types and entwine them with personification; then, coloring the words with pleasures, they gather the whole narrative of the myth, just as zodiac-sign painters depict the season of the appearance, writing in red and floral colors. And they hasten to compose material characters through phrases and forms, showing them by the work of truth itself. But these people diversify the images of myths in such a varied way; from this, a certain musical harmony and a discovery of poetic composition arise.

Plato, asking unasked, defines music as being of words; he said, 'the kind of words is twofold: the true, and the false being the other; and one must be educated in both, but first in the false ones.' For he previously said that children are easily overcome by the praise of myths. 'This, so to speak, is the whole thing false, yet in it is also truth.' Is not the beginning the greatest part of every work, and moreover, is it not something new and soft? For especially then is it molded and clothed in a type, which anyone might wish to mark for each person.

Through such things, he tries to bring forth utterances as if it were not necessary to oppose the unbridled hearings of the young, since those who are currently being marked by impressions love to have the types of bad reputation become unchangeable and difficult to erase. Therefore, it follows again: 'Will we then easily provide this?' he said, 'that the children, having heard those who have succeeded by having been fashioned by a successful myth, will receive in their souls as a great part those contrary opinions which we must expect them to have when they are perfected? Not in the least,' he has said, 'we will provide it.'

First, as it seems, we must supervise the myth-makers, and approve whichever good myth they make, and reject which one not. And let us persuade the nurses and mothers to speak to the children those which are approved, and to mold their souls with myths much more than their bodies with their hands. But now they say that the many should be cast out. Then

title: The Truth of Myths and the Belly-Myth
english: For since, asking about the proportional difference of each, Adeimantus suggested that 'in the greater [cases]' it was decided that 'even the lesser [ones] are recognized by myths,' though he did not declare knowledge of these either, he then replied again, having brought it back: 'whom both Hesiod and Homer, I said, were elegists to us; for these indeed once composed and tell myths to men, having joined them with falsehoods.'

If then Homer's epics and Hesiod's myths are judged false, which indeed especially for the sake of education cheer the hearers, and not only that but also stir up the mind toward commanded eloquence with beautiful diction, how much more should those words spoken by the possessed hag, which someone considers to be not of the kind of myth-making, be judged false, as they so sharply and even by the very name of the belly-myth direct the mind?

For if the children of the Greeks, who are precise in the naming of each matter, in Greece call myths 'false fabrications' by voice, they follow from the name the suspicion of the matter as it is primarily arranged. But Aesop's myth-makings are equal to such fabrications of myths, just as the little girls, often being mocked in childhood, play and jest with headbands (it is when they do these things, being frequently drenched in wine in the throat, and attending to the cup and the drink, they chatter without measure).
But those who consider themselves ambassadors for the ethics of philosophy cast about the kinds of poems such as these as being false myths, as is fitting.

If, therefore, the name itself is correctly assigned according to the reality of the thing, the belly-mythos seems to weave myths in the stomach; for the demon does not speak wisely from nature, but defiling the lowest parts, he infects the mind and harms the intellect, pouring out mythic fabrications composed from the stomach, and transforming into various forms, he leads the soul away with diverse disguises.

Since he is many-faced, constantly changing in shapes, he even pretends to ascend and call out from the earth, no less than before; then, rewarding the services on both sides with forms, he seems to present one person ascending to the caller, while he himself runs around here and there changing ideas, so that he may prove by deeds and words that he is a liar.

Indeed, the very faces of the dead are represented as being raised up, as it is possible to suppose from such a drama, bringing in bright faces and dark phantoms as if they were fashioned, and presenting heavy things and the scent of death as if they had been summoned from Hades, and as if they had been raised from chains for a little while, and then again passing from here to there. For he strikes the soul with terrors through these sights, fashioning pale forms, or an eye bulging or sunken, as if they were promising to breathe in the dead and then breathe out again; for the forger is accustomed to pretend by conforming to these terrible things.

But there are times when he himself changes into many forms, and there are times when he has made use of fellow demons of his own kind; he neither transfers souls from Hades, nor the spirits of the righteous, nor the angelic natures, but on the contrary, it happened to be for the purpose of playing tricks before the angels, and it was given to the best of men so that they might be struck down, being prone to fall, bursting into the earth. But this one, being driven down by a violent current from the highest, has retreated to lower things; for to God the Pantokrator alone and to the most Divine Child belongs the power to raise souls from Hades and to have them present as choirs of angels in order, which is a special distinction belonging to the Divine nature.
